parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: sum of current(s) in(to) junction or (algebraic) sum of current(s) at a junction = 0

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to electric charge when several wires meet at one point - can charge build up or disappear there?
parts.proper_answer: The sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving the junction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember charge cannot be lost**
Think of current as a flow of charge. At any junction in a circuit there is nowhere for charge to be stored, so whatever charge flows in per second must flow out per second. This is conservation of charge.

Step 2: **State the law clearly**
So you can say the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero, or more simply: $$\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}$$

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text:
State the potential difference across resistor $R$ when the slider is positioned

1. at end $X$ of the potentiometer,

2. at end $Y$ of the potentiometer.
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the two ends of resistor R in Fig. 7.1. One end is always joined to X. Where is the other end joined, and what happens to the separation of those two points as the slider moves?

Hint 2: When the slider is at X the two ends of R are joined to the same point, and when the slider is at Y, R is connected directly across the ends X and Y of the potentiometer which is across the 9.6 V battery.
parts.proper_answer: 1. at X: potential difference = $0\text{ V}$. 2. at Y: potential difference = $9.6\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See what R is connected across**
Resistor R is always connected between X and the slider. So the p.d. across R is always the same as the p.d. between X and the slider on the potentiometer wire.

Step 2: **Slider at X**
There is zero length of potentiometer wire between X and the slider, so there is no resistance and no p.d. between them. R is shorted out: $$V_R = 0\text{ V}$$

Step 3: **Slider at Y**
Now R is connected between X and Y, which is the full $800\,\Omega$ potentiometer. The potentiometer itself is connected directly across the battery of e.m.f. $9.6\text{ V}$ with negligible internal resistance. So the full battery p.d. appears across XY and across R: $$V_R = 9.6\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across resistor $R$ when the slider is positioned half-way between $X$ and $Y$.
hints: Hint 1: When the slider is half-way, split the 800 ohm potentiometer into two sections. What is the resistance from X to the slider and from the slider to Y?
Hint 2: Notice that resistor R is in parallel with only the X-to-slider section. Work out the combined resistance of that parallel pair first.

Hint 3: Now you have two resistances in series across the 9.6 V battery. Use the ratio of resistances to share the 9.6 V and find the share across the parallel combination, which is the p.d. across R.
parts.proper_answer: Parallel resistance $= 200\,\Omega$, total series resistance $= 600\,\Omega$, potential difference across R $= 3.2\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Split the potentiometer**
Half-way means half of the $800\,\Omega$ wire is on each side of the slider. So: $$R_{X\text{-slider}} = 400\,\Omega$$ $$R_{\text{slider-}Y} = 400\,\Omega$$ Resistor $R = 400\,\Omega$ is in parallel with the $400\,\Omega$ X-to-slider section.

Step 2: **Combine the parallel pair**
For two equal resistors in parallel the combined resistance is half of one. Using the formula: $$\frac{1}{R_P} = \frac{1}{400} + \frac{1}{400} = \frac{2}{400}$$ $$R_P = 200\,\Omega$$ This $200\,\Omega$ is in series with the other $400\,\Omega$ half of the potentiometer, so total resistance across the battery is: $$R_T = 200 + 400 = 600\,\Omega$$

Step 3: **Use the potential divider rule**
In series the p.d. splits in proportion to resistance. The p.d. across the parallel combination, which is the p.d. across R, is: $$V_R = 9.6 \times \frac{200}{600}$$ $$V_R = 3.2\text{ V}$$
